prime.problem: HumanEval problems are short. Real specifications chain many steps, and if a model's accuracy falls sharply with each added step, a good HumanEval score says little about longer tasks.
prime.fits: The first limitations card. It reuses pass@k and HumanEval-style prompts, but builds synthetic problems where only the number of chained steps changes.
prime.goal: Explain why a constant per-step difficulty isolates chain length, turn a per-component drop into a per-step success rate, and describe the variable-binding failure.

attend: How does the construction rule out 'the later problems were just harder'?
What per-step success rate does a 2–3× drop per component imply, and what independence assumption is behind that?
In the do_work example, which operation got attached to the wrong variable?
Why does the paper call exponential decay 'uncharacteristic of a human programmer'?

must: Every building block is one trivial line → chaining changes only the count → any drop in pass rate measures list-following, not difficulty
If each step succeeds independently with probability q → a chain of n succeeds with qⁿ → a 2–3× drop per component implies q ≈ 0.33–0.5 → pass rate decays exponentially in chain length
More operations and variables in one docstring → the model mis-binds operations to variables (subtracts from z instead of w) → the same attribute-binding failure seen in text-to-image models
Real specifications are long and system-level → decay compounds with length → the paper treats Codex as unsuited to synthesising complex systems
elevated: Measured only for Codex-12B, on string manipulation, at pass@1 → no evidence on how the decay rate changes with scale → treat the curve as a shape, not a forecast
reference: the illustrative 55% start and 2.5× rate in the card's table
Ramesh et al. (2021) on attribute binding

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences how the synthetic test is built, what it found, and what the independence model says about per-step success.
checklist: 13 one-line string operations, each with an English description
concatenate descriptions into a docstring and lines into a body
pass rate drops 2–3× per added component
separate failure: binding operations to the wrong variables

retrieve.q: Explain what makes this experiment a clean measurement of chain length, and what it would take to break that cleanness.
answer: every block is equally trivial, so only the count varies
it would break if some blocks were harder than others
or if longer chains changed the prompt format

retrieve.q: Walk through the do_work example: which steps did Codex-12B get right, which did it get wrong, and what does that show?
answer: w − 4 was never computed; z*w was computed instead
it returned z*w instead of the product of all four
operations got bound to the wrong variables

retrieve.q: Your spec has 6 independent steps. Would you give Codex one long docstring or 6 separate calls, each with a one-step docstring? What does each option cost?
answer: one docstring: pass rate ≈ qⁿ, low at n = 6
separate calls: each at the one-step rate, but you must compose and check the pieces
decomposition costs orchestration and tests for each piece

compare.q: Chaining degradation and compounding errors in agent loops both multiply per-step success. What is a 'step' in each, and which can you fix by adding checks between steps?
answer: here a step is one instruction inside a single generation
in agents a step is a whole model call
agents can verify and retry between calls; a single generation can't

compare.q: Both cards describe Codex producing code that doesn't match the docstring. Which one is a capability limit and which is a behavioural choice, by the paper's own definitions?
answer: chaining: the model can't reliably follow long lists, a capability limit
misalignment: the model can write better code but doesn't
scale is expected to help the first, not the second

predict.q: The card asks whether sampling 100 times fixes chaining. Use the qⁿ model with a 55% one-block rate and 2.5× decay, assume independent samples, and estimate pass@100 at 5 components and at 10. Does sampling rescue short chains, long chains, both, or neither? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: At 5 components pass@1 ≈ 1.41%, so pass@100 ≈ 1 − 0.9859¹⁰⁰ ≈ 76%. At 10 components pass@1 ≈ 0.0144%, so pass@100 ≈ 1.4%. Sampling rescues moderate chains (with an oracle), but the exponential wins again a few steps later. Real samples aren't independent, so the true numbers would be lower; the shape is the point.

apply.task: Fill the card's table twice more from a 55% one-block rate: once with a 2× drop per component and once with 3×, for 1–5 components. Then compute the implied per-step success q for each, and say what chain length brings each below 5%.
apply.hint: Divide by the rate each step: 55 / rᵏ⁻¹.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether 100 samples rescue a 5-step chain?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why constant per-step difficulty isolates chain length?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: per-step q → exponential decay, or more variables → mis-binding?
How long are the docstrings you'd actually give a code model at work?
What will you compare in the intent-misalignment card: can't vs won't?
